name: Games in TypeScript | Retro Cabinet
tagline: A classic games platform where nine games share one engine contract, one game loop and one save system.

keyPoints: Nine classic games (Tetris, Pacman, Space Invaders, Snake, Arkanoid, Asteroids, Columns, Frogger, Pong) behind a single game contract: each game owns its state and rules, and knows nothing about the DOM or timers.
Grid games ticking at their own speed and canvas games driven by animation frames, run by the same game loop.
Auto-save on pause or when switching tabs, best scores with their dates, per-game options.
Virtual controls on touch devices, sending the same key codes as the keyboard: games need no touch-specific code.
Each game is loaded on its first visit.

popTagline: Formerly PixelsMansion (Angular), rebuilt with Nutin to put its game architecture to the test.

overview.mainContent: Retro Cabinet is a browser arcade of classic game clones. It started as PixelsMansion, an Angular application, and was rebuilt with Nutin: the framework is now an orchestration layer around game code that doesn't depend on it.
keyPoints: A single registry of games, from which routes and home page cards are built.
Game definitions with typed options (starting level, maze, on/off settings) and a factory building the game from the chosen settings.
Versioned saves: when a game's saved fields change, its older saves are dropped instead of being restored into the wrong shape.
Keys handled by physical position, so QWERTY and AZERTY layouts both work.
A hidden tic-tac-toe against the computer, behind its own route.
overview.after: As with PixelsMansion, games are features: the focus is the architecture that lets them coexist.

purpose.title: Purpose
keyPoints: To check that the game architecture designed with Angular holds without a full framework.
To keep game rules testable in isolation, away from rendering and timing.
To use Nutin on an application with real-time constraints.

constraints.title: Constraints
keyPoints: Games are pure logic: no DOM, no timers, no storage access.
One loop, one save system and one control scheme for every game.
Adding a game means writing its rules and one registry entry.

choices.title: A narrow contract between games and the view
choices.mainContent: Every game implements the same interface: reset, tick, key handling, and optional snapshot / restore for saves. The view drives it and renders what it exposes: a grid of cells, or a canvas drawing.
choices.after: Games remain unit-testable without a browser.

choices.title: Grid and canvas games under one loop
choices.mainContent: Grid games tick on chained timeouts, reading their speed again before every tick so a level-up applies immediately. Canvas games tick on animation frames, with a capped time step so a stalled frame can't make a ball go through bricks.

choices.title: Defensive persistence
choices.mainContent: Stored data is treated as untrusted: every reader checks the shape it gets and treats anything else as nothing stored. Saves carry a version per game.

challenges.title: Porting without carrying the framework over
challenges.mainContent: PixelsMansion relied on Angular signals for change propagation. Rebuilding it with Nutin meant making updates explicit, which moved logic out of the UI layer and into the games themselves.

challenges.title: Touch input
challenges.mainContent: Touch controls (a D-pad, or a stick for steering games like Snake) send the same key codes as the keyboard, with an optional repeat for held directions.
challenges.after: Input stays a single concern for the games.

keyPoints: An architecture is validated by moving it, not by building it once.
Keeping game logic free of rendering made both the port and the tests easier.
Saved data needs versioning as soon as it outlives a release.
